claims.text: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) has an alpha-plus-beta dual-phase microstructure.
TC4 has low hardness under extreme loading.
TC4 has poor friction and wear performance under extreme loading.
A thin, functionally graded refractory HEA coating can be deposited on TC4 by magnetron sputtering.
The deposited coating can transition smoothly in composition from a TC4-interfacing layer to a refractory HEA surface layer.
The graded coating will form a strong interface with TC4.
The graded interface will minimize residual stresses.
The graded interface will prevent the formation of brittle intermetallic phases.
The graded interface will produce strong metallurgical bonding between the coating and TC4.
A gradual compositional transition reduces thermal mismatch between the TC4 substrate and the refractory HEA layer.
A gradual compositional transition reduces mechanical mismatch between the TC4 substrate and the refractory HEA layer.
Avoiding a sharp coating-substrate interface reduces cracking and delamination.
Multi-element solid-solution strengthening in the refractory HEA layer provides high surface hardness.
Multi-element solid-solution strengthening in the refractory HEA layer improves wear resistance.
The coated TC4 will have higher surface hardness than untreated TC4.
The coated TC4 will have a significantly lower wear rate than untreated TC4 under high-contact-stress wear.
The coating will preserve the beneficial bulk properties of TC4.
Coating thicknesses exceeding tens of micrometers may alter the TC4 substrate and limit effectiveness.
Thermal cycling beyond the coating's designed range may limit its effectiveness.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts both increased hardness and reduced wear, but the falsification rule requires both hardness improvement to be inadequate and wear reduction to fail. Failure of only one of the two predicted benefits would therefore not falsify the corresponding conjunctive prediction.
